Another colleague's birthday is coming up and they want to buy them a pig and I don't really agree. WIBTA if I don't contribute? I really wish this was a joke but let me explain. This colleague of mine is about to turn 40. We will call them George if that's okay. Nothing against her she is a great person. Now George still lives at home with their parents and owns a dog. They are going through the phase of desperately dating around, and they have always wanted a micro pig. My colleagues love to celebrate birthdays. They bought me fish, bless them, for my 20th birthday because I was very lonely at the time as I had just moved out from my parents house etc. I really appreciated the thought and I love my fish dearly, but sometimes I feel a little bit tied down by them, as I'm not always at home (I spend a lot of time around my boyfriend 's house) and one day I eventually want to move away and that may be an issue with fish as if be looking to go to another house share. Don't get me wrong I really really appreciated the thought, but I don't think they took into consideration the commitment it takes to look after an animal. They did mean we'll though. Although I expressed slight interest in what I would hypothetically name an axolotl before my birthday, I never ever expected to see fish when I walked into my room. I am currently in a house share with a colleague, as it was the only viable option at the time. Back to George, my concern is they still live at home and it really isn't fair on their parents to bring a surprise pig into the house. I'm also concerned about how the pig will interact with the dog. If course I want to celebrate their birthday, but I just simply don't agree with buying someone a micro pig without taking into consideration the commitments that go into looking after them. Besides little guppies are very different to a micro pig. So will I be the asshole if I just buy my own gift for them?

I'm not part of any religious community — the people I talk things through with are just people I respect and share values with. Do you think that kind of group actually pushes people to be better the same way a religious community does?

It’s a great question, and one that touches on a lot of research about how people grow, learn, and stay motivated. Whether a group is framed as a “religious community” or simply a circle of friends who share values, the underlying mechanisms that help people become better versions of themselves are often the same. Below is a quick rundown of what tends to work, why it matters, and how you can make the most of a secular, values‑based community. --- ## 1. The Core Ingredients of a “Good” Community | Ingredient | Why it matters | How it shows up in a secular group | |------------|----------------|------------------------------------| | **Shared values & purpose** | Gives members a common north star. | A mission statement, a set of guiding principles, or a shared vision (e.g., “We strive to be compassionate, curious, and courageous”). | | **Accountability** | Encourages follow‑through and honest self‑reflection. | Regular check‑ins, peer‑review of goals, or a “buddy system” where you hold each other to commitments. | | **Support & empathy** | Reduces isolation, boosts resilience. | Listening circles, emotional check‑ins, or simply being there when someone’s going through a tough time. | | **Norms & rituals** | Reinforces identity and consistency. | Weekly meetings, shared reading, or a ritual of sharing wins and lessons learned. | | **Openness to growth** | Keeps the group dynamic and prevents stagnation. | Encouraging experimentation, celebrating failures as learning moments, or rotating leadership roles. | --- ## 2. How These Ingredients Push People to Be Better 1. **Social Identity Theory** When you identify strongly with a group, you’re more likely to adopt its norms. If the group values honesty, you’ll be more honest; if it values continuous learning, you’ll seek out new knowledge. 2. **Normative Influence** People tend to conform to what they see others doing. If most members are practicing gratitude or setting ambitious goals, you’ll be nudged to do the same. 3. **Cognitive Dissonance** When your actions conflict with the group’s values, you experience discomfort. To reduce that, you either change your behavior or your beliefs. In a supportive environment, the former is usually easier. 4. **Positive Feedback Loops** Small wins are celebrated, which boosts confidence and encourages further effort. Over time, the group’s collective success becomes a self‑reinforcing cycle. 5. **Emotional Contagion** Positive emotions (hope, excitement, curiosity) spread through social networks. A group that radiates optimism can lift everyone’s mood and motivation. --- ## 3. Secular Communities vs. Religious Communities | Aspect | Religious Community | Secular Values‑Based Community | |--------|---------------------|--------------------------------| | **Source of Authority** | Divine or sacred texts | Shared human experience, collective wisdom | | **Rituals** | Prayer, sacraments, liturgy | Meetings, shared reading, community projects | | **Accountability** | Moral law, confession | Peer review, goal‑setting, mutual support | | **Identity** | Spiritual identity | Ethical or philosophical identity | | **Potential Pitfalls** | Dogma, exclusion, hierarchy | Groupthink, lack of structure, ambiguity | Both can be powerful, but secular groups often have more flexibility to adapt norms, experiment with new practices, and remain inclusive of diverse viewpoints. That said, they can also lack the “spiritual weight” that some people find motivating. The key is to design the group so that its values feel meaningful and its rituals feel authentic. --- ## 4. Practical Tips for Building or Joining a Values‑Based Group 1. **Define Your Core Values** Write down 3–5 values that resonate with you (e.g., integrity, curiosity, generosity). Share them with potential members and see if they align. 2. **Create a Simple Mission Statement** A one‑sentence purpose can guide decisions and keep the group focused. 3. **Set Up Regular Check‑Ins** Even a 15‑minute weekly call can keep momentum. Use a shared calendar or a simple group chat. 4. **Establish Accountability Mechanisms** Pair up members as “accountability partners.” They can set goals, share progress, and gently push each other. 5. **Celebrate Wins and Learn from Failures** Make it a habit to share both successes and setbacks. This builds a culture of growth rather than judgment. 6. **Invite Guest Speakers or Workshops** Fresh perspectives can keep the group dynamic and prevent stagnation. 7. **Keep the Door Open** Allow new members to join without a formal initiation. The more diverse the group, the richer the learning. --- ## 5. Potential Challenges and How to Mitigate Them | Challenge | Why it Happens | Mitigation | |-----------|----------------|------------| | **Groupthink** | Desire for harmony leads to conformity. | Encourage dissenting opinions, rotate discussion leaders. | | **Uneven Participation** | Some members dominate, others stay silent. | Set speaking turns, use anonymous feedback tools. | | **Burnout** | Over‑commitment to group activities. | Set realistic expectations, respect personal boundaries. | | **Conflict** | Differing interpretations of values. | Establish a conflict‑resolution protocol (e.g., mediation, open dialogue). | --- ## 6. Bottom Line A secular community that shares values can be just as effective—if not more so—than a religious one in encouraging personal growth. The key is intentionality: clearly articulated values, structured accountability, supportive rituals, and a culture that celebrates both progress and learning from setbacks. If you’re already part of such a group, you’re likely benefiting from these mechanisms. If you’re looking to create or join one, start with a small, focused circle and let the community evolve organically around shared purpose. Feel free to share more about the group you’re in or the values you’re hoping to cultivate, and I can help you tailor these ideas even further!
